practice_description.medium: Software, drawing, games, generative text, web art, writing
practice_description.practice_summary: Everest Pipkin is an artist and tool-maker whose practice centers on commons-oriented software, generative text, drawing, and critical engagement with extractive technology. They build tools that embody ethical positions about openness, sustainability, and collective ownership.
practice_description.methodology: Pipkin works across drawing, programming, and writing, often creating tools and games that are themselves artworks. Their methodology is rooted in careful material consideration — choosing technologies that align with ethical commitments (low-energy, open-source, non-extractive). They maintain a critical perspective on AI, large-scale data harvesting, and platform capitalism, articulated through both artistic works and influential essays. Their process is slow, deliberate, and attentive to the politics embedded in technical choices.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Pipkin's practice of building commons-oriented tools as artworks directly models a mode of art-making where infrastructure and creative expression are inseparable — essential for a graph-curated exhibition treating system design as medium.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. Their generative text works, drawing tools, and game engines can function as substrate layers. Works like Lacework produce outputs that could be embedded in larger compositions.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Partially. Some works (particularly generative text pieces) create meaning through relational juxtaposition of elements. The tool-making practice creates infrastructure that enables relational composition by others.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Several works are generative and produce different outputs on each encounter. Browser-based pieces often incorporate randomness and recombination. However, the emphasis is on considered, intentional generation rather than autonomous evolution.

works.title: The Barnacle Goose Experiment
works.description: A collaborative wiki-novel built in a custom engine where readers and writers co-create a branching, evolving narrative. Explores collective authorship and commons-based creative production.
works.relevance: Directly models collective, relational content creation — a community-authored graph of narrative where meaning emerges from connections and contributions.

works.title: Lacework
works.description: A generative drawing tool that creates intricate lace-like patterns through algorithmic processes, released as open-source software.
works.relevance: Exemplifies tool-as-artwork with commons orientation. The generative outputs are themselves artworks that could serve as visual substrate in a composed exhibition.

works.title: On Gathering (essay)
works.description: An influential essay critiquing large-scale dataset collection practices in AI/ML, arguing for ethical data gathering that respects consent and commons principles.
works.relevance: Provides critical theoretical framework for how A(DAI) should approach data provenance, consent, and the ethics of building a collective intelligence commons.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Pipkin treats the design of tools, platforms, and infrastructure as artistic medium. The ethical and political commitments embedded in their software — open licensing, low energy use, non-extraction — are aesthetic choices as much as moral ones.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Multiple open-source tools and game engines. The Barnacle Goose Experiment's collaborative wiki platform. Various generative text and drawing systems released as commons infrastructure.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Deeply commons-oriented at every level. Open-source tool releases, critical writing against data enclosure, explicit advocacy for non-extractive technology. Their practice is one of the strongest examples of commons-as-medium in contemporary digital art.

governance_model.governance_detail: Solo practice with participatory elements. The Barnacle Goose Experiment distributes authorial governance to participants. Tool releases invite community contribution. No formal governance structure but strong ethical framework guiding decisions.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Consent is a central concern. Their critical writing explicitly addresses consent in data gathering. Participatory works are designed with informed, voluntary participation. They advocate against scraping and non-consensual data collection.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo for tools and essays, collaborative/distributed for participatory projects like Barnacle Goose. Open-source releases enable community co-authorship.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Generative works produce different outputs on each encounter. Web-based pieces are durational in that they persist and can be revisited. The Barnacle Goose Experiment evolves through community contribution over time.

data_materiality.data_sources: Self-generated datasets, hand-curated text corpora, participant contributions, public domain texts. Deliberately avoids scraped data from non-consenting sources.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Ethically sourced — consented, self-generated, or public domain. Pipkin is one of the most vocal advocates for ethical data provenance in the digital arts.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Not a primary focus, and in fact Pipkin is critically skeptical of large-scale embedding/ML systems due to their extractive data practices. Some generative text work engages with semantic space at a smaller, more intentional scale.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes — practice spans drawing, text, code, games, and writing, though not unified through embedding spaces.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works primarily encountered through web browsers and screens. Some gallery installations and performative readings. The web is the primary exhibition space, consistent with commons principles of open access.

interoperability.composability: Moderate. Tools produce standard outputs (images, text files) that can feed into other processes. Open-source code is forkable and adaptable. Not explicitly designed as modular pipeline components but amenable to integration.

technical_approach.stack: JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS, custom game engines, generative algorithms, minimal/low-dependency approaches reflecting sustainability commitments

network_position.scene_affiliation: Net art, indie games, critical tech art, digital commons movement, creative coding community. Connected to both art world and tech ethics discourse.
network_position.connections: Sam Lavigne (shared tool-making and commons ethos), Darius Kazemi (bot/generative art community), broader indie game and net art communities

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Pipkin's critical perspective on extractive technology and their commons-first practice provide an essential ethical compass for A(DAI). Their writing on data gathering directly informs how A(DAI) should approach consent and provenance. They could serve as a critical friend who tests whether A(DAI) lives up to its commons commitments.
